summary:
Andrew Garvin, co-founder of Metronome (recently acquired by Stripe in its largest deal), presents a live demo titled 'How to avoid disaster when vibe-coding a billing engine.' He frames the talk around the risks of letting coding agents autonomously run a complex usage-billing platform and argues for agent-accelerated test environments with a human in the loop. The demo uses Stripe Projects, a CLI orchestrator launched the same week as the Metronome acquisition, to provision a sandbox that mimics Lovable's pricing model. The stack includes Stripe, Vercel, Postgres, and a Metronome billing agent, all driven by a single natural-language prompt.

Metronome's guardrails for agent-driven setup include skills files that carry the hard-won API context, deliberately verbose error messages so the agent can self-correct, and a deliberate decision to keep a human in the loop rather than ship to production autonomously. On the Metronome side, the resulting sandbox shows a customer with lifetime spend populated by the agent, a draft invoice structured exactly like Lovable's pricing model (credit-only with monthly auto-recharge), separately scoped credit pools for builds, plan mode, cloud, and AI gateway calls, and metered usage drawing down credits with overage invoiced at period end.

Garvin introduces a three-part framework: agent as product (requiring metered usage pricing), agent as buyer (Stripe Projects procuring its own infrastructure), and agent as user, the disruptive category where one agent replaces many human seats. He notes that coding vendors like Cognition, Cursor, OpenAI, and Anthropic are adopting CSP-style commit structures (prepaid, postpaid, customer-specific offers) and points to HubSpot's EMEA transition from seats to credits as evidence that agent-as-user economics is reshaping incumbent SaaS pricing. He closes by inviting developers to try Stripe Projects themselves, noting providers like Vercel and Hugging Face are onboarding to make their products more discoverable to agents.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction: Metronome, Stripe, and the Stripe Projects orchestrator
sections.summary: Garvin introduces himself as a Metronome co-founder, notes Stripe's acquisition of Metronome as its largest deal, and frames the talk as a joint demo with the Stripe team. He describes Stripe Projects as a CLI-based orchestrator that provisions a Stripe account plus backend services including a Metronome billing agent.

sections.title: Thesis: avoiding disaster when vibe coding a billing engine
sections.summary: He states the thesis explicitly: usage billing is deep, business-critical, and prone to failure when operated end-to-end by a coding agent. Metronome is investing in better developer experience, including metering, credit models, and agent-wallet controls to prevent runaway spend.

sections.title: Live demo: initializing Stripe Projects and typing the Lovable prompt
sections.summary: Garvin runs a live CLI demo, hits a brief 'not initialized' hiccup, and then submits a single natural-language prompt instructing the system to create a Metronome billing engine mimicking Lovable's prepaid-credit auto-recharge pricing model.

sections.title: Skills files, verbose errors, and the human-in-the-loop philosophy
sections.summary: He explains the guardrails: portable, extensible skills files that give agents API context; deliberately verbose error messages so the agent can self-correct; and a deliberate decision to keep a human in the loop, targeting test/sandbox mode rather than unsupervised production shipping. Stripe Projects also drives usage into Metronome so the customer can see what a live customer looks like.

sections.title: Three agent roles: product, buyer, and user
sections.summary: Garvin introduces a framework separating agent-as-product (requiring metered/usage pricing), agent-as-buyer (Stripe Projects procuring its own infrastructure), and agent-as-user. The third category is the disruptive one, with HubSpot cited as moving from seats to credits in EMEA because a single agent can replace many human seats.

sections.title: Why agent-as-user economics breaks seat-based pricing
sections.summary: He expands on agent-as-user dynamics with examples from last week's Andreessen demo day, where all five companies were sales-led agents operating platforms like SAP and invoicing systems, concentrating value into a single agent user and accelerating the shift to credits-based pricing.

sections.title: Setup complete and what comes next
sections.summary: The demo setup finishes and the sandbox is ready. Garvin teases the upcoming inspection of the agent's actual output, including a customer record, flowing metered usage, and a draft invoice broken into scoped credit pools for builds, plan mode, cloud, and gateway calls, while flagging auto-recharge, credit expiry, and overage as the areas where companies typically hurt themselves.

sections.title: Pricing models and CSP-style commit structures
sections.summary: Garvin notes he is a good person to talk to about agentic pricing models, observes that the credits-based model has been dominant since OpenAI launched their prepaid-credit auto-recharge model through Metronome, and points out that coding vendors like Cognition, Cursor, OpenAI, and Anthropic are adopting CSP-style commit structures (prepaid commitments, postpaid commitments, and customer-specific offers) similar to what CSPs have used for the past 10 years.

sections.title: Inspecting the Metronome sandbox: customer, usage, and credit objects
sections.summary: Garvin opens the Metronome instance and walks through the primitives the agent populated. The human onboarding wizard is bypassed because the agent set up the environment. The customer pane shows auto-populated lifetime spend, the usage drawer shows meter activity for testing purposes, and a draft invoice replicates Lovable's pricing model: credit-only with monthly auto-recharge, scoped credit pools per usage type, first-class credit objects that drew down against the initial period's credits, and an invoice for any overspend at period end.

sections.title: Scoped credit pools and how the agent replicated Lovable's model
sections.summary: He drills into each component of the draft invoice: build credits, plan mode credits, cloud credits, and AI gateway credits, which is exactly how Lovable's pricing model is structured. The only coaching required was describing in natural language to replicate the Lovable pricing model, with the skills files and verbose errors guiding the agent through the rest.

sections.title: What this suggests beyond billing, and how to try it
sections.summary: Garvin summarizes what was built: a Stripe instance, a Metronome instance via Stripe Projects, and a demo instance of Metronome with a real pricing model live in production, ready for further testing and tweaking. He argues the framework applies more broadly to agentic development beyond Stripe, reiterating the three agent roles and the need to coach agents to operate effectively in difficult environments. He closes by inviting developers to try Stripe Projects themselves, noting providers like Vercel and Hugging Face are onboarding to make their products more discoverable to agents operating in the Stripe system.

demonstrations: Live initialization of Stripe Projects via CLI to provision a sandbox Stripe account plus backend services including a Metronome billing agent.
Typing a single natural-language prompt asking Metronome to create a billing engine mimicking Lovable's pricing model.
Surfacing of a transient 'It's not initialized' error during the live demo before successful setup.
On-screen skills file visible during the demo, showing context given to the agent.
Verbose error message rendered in the CLI designed for agent self-correction.

Inspection of the resulting Metronome sandbox: customer pane with auto-populated lifetime spend, usage drawer, and a draft invoice with scoped credit pools for builds, plan mode, cloud, and AI gateway.
Drilling into each credit component to show the credit draw-down and overage invoice at period end, matching Lovable's credit-only auto-recharge model.
limitations: The demo was explicitly framed as a test/sandbox environment, not production.
A live demo hiccup ('It's not initialized') briefly interrupted the setup.
The on-stage prompt targeted a sandbox; real production billing edge cases (auto-recharge rules, credit expiry, overage handling) are noted as the harder problems companies usually get wrong.
The Metronome inspection stayed at the level of showing primitives; deeper configuration of auto-recharge, credit expiry, and overage logic was not exercised on stage.

Metronome has metered API calls for OpenAI and Anthropic since before those companies had revenue.

HubSpot is currently on a path to transform from seat-based to credits-based, starting in EMEA where they have dramatically lowered their seats-based price.
